chapters.title: Chapter 2: How Deals Get Done in India

lessons.title: Schemes of Arrangement: Board Approval, SEBI, NCLT, and the Shareholder Vote

children.text: HDFC announced its merger with HDFC Bank on 4 April 2022. HDFC Ltd shareholders did not receive HDFC Bank shares until July 2023, fifteen months later. Nothing was broken in between. That is simply how long a large scheme of arrangement takes to clear the board, the stock exchanges, SEBI, sector regulators, shareholders, creditors and the National Company Law Tribunal. If you hold a stock going through a scheme, knowing these stages tells you where the deal stands, what can still derail it and when your vote actually counts.

body.text: A deal announcement is a proposal, not a done deal. A scheme becomes real only after it clears every gate in sequence: board, stock exchanges and SEBI, shareholders and creditors, and finally the NCLT. Each gate is a point where the terms can be questioned or the deal can die.

children.text: What a Scheme of Arrangement Is

A scheme of arrangement is a legal document, often running to a hundred pages or more, that sets out exactly how a merger, demerger or other restructuring will work: which assets and liabilities move, from which
appointed date

, at what swap or entitlement ratio, and what happens to employees and creditors. It is governed by Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013, and for listed companies also by SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations. Once the
NCLT
sanctions it, it binds every shareholder and creditor, including those who voted against it.

markDefs.definition: The date from which the scheme is treated as effective for accounting purposes. It is often earlier than the date the scheme legally takes effect.

National Company Law Tribunal. The quasi-judicial body that hears and sanctions schemes of arrangement under the Companies Act, 2013, with benches in cities including Mumbai, New Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata and Ahmedabad.

body.text: The binding effect is the whole point. A scheme lets a company restructure without needing every single shareholder to agree. That is also why the law builds in so many approvals and objection rights before the NCLT signs off: once it does, the minority is carried along.

children.text: The Five Gates, in Order
Gate 1: Board approval.

The board approves the draft scheme, supported by a valuation report from an independent registered valuer and a fairness opinion from an independent SEBI-registered merchant banker. For listed companies, the audit committee and a committee of independent directors must also report on the scheme, including whether it is fair to minority shareholders. The company discloses the board outcome to BSE and NSE the same day.
Gate 2: Stock exchanges and SEBI.

Under Regulation 37 of the LODR Regulations, a listed company files the draft scheme with the stock exchanges before approaching the NCLT. The exchanges examine it, forward it to SEBI for comments, and then issue an
observation letter
. Sector regulators such as the RBI for banks and NBFCs, and the Competition Commission of India for large deals, give their approvals in parallel.

markDefs.definition: The letter issued by a stock exchange, after incorporating SEBI's comments, stating that it has no adverse observations or listing the conditions the company must meet. Without it, a listed company cannot take its scheme to the NCLT.

children.text: Gate 3: NCLT first motion.

The company applies to the NCLT, which directs it to hold meetings of shareholders and creditors, or dispenses with some meetings if consents are already in hand. Notices also go to the Central Government, the Registrar of Companies, the income tax authorities and other relevant regulators, who get 30 days to raise objections.
Gate 4: Shareholder and creditor votes.
This is where you get a say. Listed companies must offer e-voting, so you can vote through the NSDL or CDSL e-voting platform or your broker's link without attending the meeting.
Gate 5: NCLT second motion and sanction.

The company petitions the NCLT to sanction the scheme. The tribunal hears any objections and passes a sanction order under Section 232. The scheme takes legal effect once the certified order is filed with the Registrar of Companies, which must happen within 30 days. Only then does the company fix a record date and issue new shares.

body.title: The HDFC and HDFC Bank scheme, gate by gate

events.title: Boards approve the scheme
events.description: Both boards approve the merger and the swap ratio of 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares. The announcement goes to BSE and NSE the same day.

events.title: Stock exchanges and RBI clear the scheme
events.description: BSE and NSE issue their observation letters with SEBI's comments, and the RBI gives its approval, subject to conditions.

events.title: Shareholders vote
events.description: NCLT-convened meetings of both companies' shareholders approve the scheme by an overwhelming majority.

events.title: NCLT Mumbai sanctions the scheme
events.description: The tribunal passes its sanction order after the remaining regulatory approvals are in place.

events.title: Merger becomes effective
events.description: HDFC Ltd ceases to exist. Shareholders on the 13 July 2023 record date receive HDFC Bank shares.

body.text: Fifteen months was fast for a deal that size. Schemes involving several companies, disputes or objections can take two years or more. Until the NCLT sanctions the scheme, do not treat the swap ratio as money in the bank, and be wary of anyone telling you a deal is "certain".

children.text: How the Shareholder Vote Works

Under Section 230(6) of the Companies Act, a scheme passes a class meeting only if it wins a majority in number of those voting, and that majority also represents at least three-fourths in value of the votes cast. "In value" means counted by shares, so one shareholder with a crore shares outweighs a thousand shareholders with ten shares each on this test.

body.latex: \text{Value test passes if } \frac{\text{Shares voted in favour}}{\text{Total shares voted}} \geq 75\%
body.caption: Only votes actually cast count. Shares that do not vote are ignored in both the numerator and the denominator.

stats.label: Right to object at NCLT
stats.context: Or 5% of total outstanding debt for creditors

stats.label: Regulator objection window
stats.context: From receiving notice of the scheme

body.title: Did the scheme pass the value test?
body.prompt: At the shareholder meeting of a fictional listed company, Tapti Polymers, 8.2 crore shares are voted in favour of a merger scheme and 3.1 crore shares against. What percentage of the shares voted were in favour? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Total shares voted = 8.2 crore + 3.1 crore = 11.3 crore. In favour = 8.2 ÷ 11.3 × 100 = 72.57%, which rounds to 72.6%. That is below 75%, so the scheme fails the value test even though far more shares voted for it than against it.

children.text: The Protection That Matters Most: Majority of the Minority

Promoters often own more than 50% of an Indian listed company. On the 75% value test alone, a promoter holding 70% would need only a small slice of public support. So SEBI adds a second condition for schemes where promoters could benefit at the expense of public shareholders, such as when promoters get additional shares, when a promoter-owned unlisted company merges into the listed one, or when the counterparty is a related party. In those cases, the scheme can go ahead only if
public shareholders
cast more votes in favour than against it. Promoter votes do not count on this test.

markDefs.definition: All shareholders other than the promoter and promoter group. This includes retail investors, mutual funds, foreign portfolio investors and insurance companies.

body.title: Tapti Polymers scheme vote: overall vs public shareholders only
Majority of the minority
body.question: In a revised Tapti Polymers scheme, a promoter-owned private company merges into the listed company. Promoters vote 6.0 crore shares in favour. Public shareholders vote 1.2 crore shares in favour and 1.8 crore against. Overall, 7.2 crore of 9.0 crore shares voted, or 80%, are in favour. What happens?
options: The scheme passes because 80% is above the 75% value test
The scheme passes because promoters hold a majority of the company
The scheme cannot be acted upon because public shareholders cast more votes against it than in favour
The vote is invalid because promoters are not allowed to vote at all
body.explanation: The overall value test is met at 80%, but because a promoter-owned company is merging in, SEBI's public shareholder condition applies. Public votes against (1.8 crore) exceed public votes in favour (1.2 crore), so the scheme cannot go ahead. This is exactly the situation where your vote as a retail investor has real weight.

body.title: The exchange's verdict
body.textWithBlank: Before a listed company can take its scheme to the NCLT, it needs an ___ letter from the stock exchanges, issued after SEBI's comments.
body.explanation: The observation letter, often reported as a no-objection letter, confirms the exchanges and SEBI have reviewed the scheme. Any conditions in it must be disclosed to shareholders before they vote.

children.text: The Shortcut: Fast-Track Mergers

body.title: Regular NCLT route vs fast-track merger under Section 233

columns.label: Regular route (Sections 230 to 232)
points: Available for any company, including large listed companies
Approved by the NCLT after first and second motions
Shareholder approval: majority in number and three-fourths in value of votes cast
Stock exchange and SEBI review for listed companies

columns.label: Fast-track route (Section 233)
points: Limited to specified cases, such as small companies, startups, and a holding company with its wholly owned subsidiary
Approved by the Regional Director of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, not the NCLT
Needs approval from members holding at least 90% of total shares
Needs creditors holding nine-tenths in value to approve

children.text: As a listed company investor, you will mostly see fast-track mergers when a listed company absorbs its own wholly owned subsidiaries. These do not change your holding, because no new shares go to outside shareholders.

body.title: Three documents worth reading before you vote

children.text: The valuation report.
Prepared by a registered valuer, it shows how each company was valued, which methods were used, what weight each method got and how the swap ratio was derived. Lesson 2.2 teaches you how to read it.
The fairness opinion.
A merchant banker's view that the swap ratio is fair to shareholders. It is short and rarely critical, so read it for its assumptions and limitations, not its conclusion.
The independent directors' report.
It explains why the committee considers the scheme in the interest of minority shareholders. A vague report that simply repeats management's rationale tells you something too.
All three are attached to the company's Regulation 37 filing on the BSE and NSE websites, and to the notice of the NCLT-convened meeting.

body.title: The e-voting email
body.scenario: You hold 300 shares of a fictional listed company, Godavari Consumer Ltd, whose promoters own 62%. You receive an email from CDSL with an e-voting link for an NCLT-convened meeting to approve the merger of Godavari Organics Pvt Ltd, a private company fully owned by the promoter family, into Godavari Consumer. The promoters will receive new shares that take their holding to 68%. Voting closes in six days.
body.prompt: How much does your vote matter here, and what would you do before voting?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Your vote matters more than usual. A promoter-owned private company merging into the listed company, with promoters receiving extra shares, is exactly the kind of scheme where SEBI requires public shareholders' votes in favour to exceed their votes against. Promoter votes do not decide this test.
2. Read the valuation report. The key question is whether Godavari Organics has been valued too richly, since every rupee of excess valuation means more shares for promoters and dilution for you.
3. Read the independent directors' report and the fairness opinion for how they justify the ratio for minority shareholders.
4. Check the proxy advisors. Firms such as IiAS, InGovern and SES publish voting recommendations on major schemes, and mutual funds disclose how they voted.
5. Vote. Many retail investors ignore e-voting emails, which leaves the outcome to institutions. If you think the terms are unfair, vote against, and if you hold 10% or more with others, you can also object before the NCLT.

body.title: Tracking a scheme you are invested in
steps: Note the board approval date and read the scheme, valuation report and fairness opinion
Watch for the stock exchange observation letter and any conditions SEBI attached
Check which sector regulators must approve, such as the RBI or CCI
Look out for the NCLT meeting notice and e-voting window, and vote
Check whether the public shareholder majority condition applies
Track the NCLT sanction, the effective date and the record date announcement

body.label: National Company Law Tribunal
body.description: Search cause lists and orders by company name to see where a scheme stands at its NCLT bench.

cards.definition: A legal plan under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 for mergers, demergers and restructurings, binding on all shareholders and creditors once sanctioned by the NCLT.
The submission of a listed company's draft scheme to the stock exchanges under SEBI's LODR Regulations, before approaching the NCLT.
The stock exchange's response to a draft scheme after SEBI's comments, which a listed company needs before going to the NCLT.
The NCLT application in which the tribunal directs meetings of shareholders and creditors.
The petition for final sanction of the scheme after the meetings are held.
The Section 230(6) requirement that votes in favour represent at least 75% of the shares voted.
SEBI's condition that, in specified schemes, public shareholders' votes in favour must exceed their votes against.
A simplified merger under Section 233 for specified cases, approved by the Regional Director instead of the NCLT.

points: A scheme of arrangement moves through five gates: board, stock exchanges and SEBI, NCLT first motion, shareholder and creditor votes, and NCLT sanction.
Large schemes take a year or more. HDFC's merger took fifteen months from announcement to effective date.
A scheme needs a majority in number and at least three-fourths in value of the votes cast. Only votes actually cast count.
When promoters could benefit, SEBI also requires public shareholders' votes in favour to exceed their votes against, which gives retail votes real weight.
Only holders of 10% of shares, or creditors with 5% of outstanding debt, can object to a scheme before the NCLT.
Read the valuation report, fairness opinion and independent directors' report before you vote.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or legal advice. Tapti Polymers, Godavari Consumer and Godavari Organics are fictional. The legal thresholds described are simplified summaries of the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI regulations as generally applied, and specific schemes can involve additional conditions. Dates for the HDFC scheme are from public disclosures. Always read the actual scheme documents and meeting notice before voting.
